idiom_name: mod tree per crate: private by default, pub / pub(crate) / pub(super) for the published surface
implementation_notes: Rust builds the module into the language: mod declares a unit (inline or in a same-named file), items are private to their module and its descendants by default, and pub, pub(crate), pub(super) and pub(in path) open them piecemeal - the closest thing to an enforced published interface among mainstream languages. Re-exports (pub use) let a module present a facade that differs from its internal file layout, which is how a domain module keeps its public API small while the implementation stays nested and changeable. When a module must be a hard boundary for other projects, promote it to its own crate or workspace member: crates cannot see each other's private items at all, at the cost of a versioned dependency.
pitfalls: Privacy is one-way by design: a child module may use its ancestors' items but a parent cannot reach a child's private items, so helper modules must be declared where their users are or re-exported.
pub use can widen the surface by accident: re-exporting an internal module turns it into public API that later churn cannot remove without a breaking change.
Splitting one concept into a separate crate for a harder boundary brings the orphan rule, duplicated dependency versions and slower builds - do it for distribution, not for tidiness.
